%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
Large-scale LLM serving is increasingly shaped by the convergence of sparse MoE base models and LoRA-based multi-tenant adaptation. In multi-LoRA MoE serving, tenant-specific LoRA modules are attached to sparsely activated expert layers, creating a decode-time serving regime in which the effective unit of access and reuse is a joint expert--LoRA object rather than an expert or adapter alone. Our trace-driven analysis shows that this shift weakens hot-set concentration, reduces the effectiveness of cache scaling, and pushes the remaining performance loss into the latency tail.

We present CoLoRA, a decode-time runtime for multi-LoRA MoE serving that treats GPU-cold misses as an execution-first recovery problem rather than a promotion-first caching problem. CoLoRA adopts a residency-aware hot/cold dual-path design: GPU-resident objects remain on the hot path, while GPU-cold objects are handled through a CPU cold path that computes only the LoRA residual from host-resident weights and merges it back for the current token. CoLoRA further incorporates deferred promotion and selective temporal predispatch to improve future reuse and partially overlap cold-path latency. Our evaluation shows that CoLoRA improves the resilience of multi-LoRA MoE decode serving under realistic cache pressure by reducing tail-latency inflation while preserving the GPU as the primary engine for hot objects and base-model execution.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large-scale LLM serving is increasingly shaped by the convergence of two trends: sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) base models~\cite{todo:moe-llm} and LoRA-based multi-tenant adaptation~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. In practice, these trends meet in \emph{multi-LoRA MoE serving}. While existing multi-LoRA systems target dense modules such as attention layers and shared FFNs, they do directly address adaptation on sparsely activated MoE expert layers~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. This gap is critical: MoE expert FFN blocks comprise the majority of model capacity, making them the natural target for tenant-specific specialization~\cite{todo:moe-knowledge-capacity, schulman2025lora}. This combination couples the compute efficiency of MoE with the parameter efficiency of LoRA. However, it creates a new serving regime in which request-time sparse routing and tenant-specific adapter selection jointly shape the active weights. This significantly enlarges and diversifies the inference working set, rendering it difficult to manage with existing caching strategies.
% v2: Large-scale LLM serving is increasingly shaped by the convergence of two trends that are individually effective but jointly nontrivial to serve: sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) base models~\cite{todo:moe-llm} and LoRA-based multi-tenant adaptation~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. In practice, these trends naturally meet in \emph{multi-LoRA MoE serving}. Existing multi-LoRA serving systems, however, are primarily designed for dense backbones and do not directly address adaptation on sparsely activated MoE expert layers~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. Such adaptation is both natural and important: MoE expert FFN blocks comprise a large fraction of model capacity and are a natural target for tenant-specific specialization~\cite{todo:moe-knowledge-capacity, schulman2025lora}. The resulting combination is attractive because it couples the compute efficiency of MoE with the parameter efficiency of LoRA. At the same time, it creates a new serving regime in which request-time sparse routing and tenant-specific adapter selection jointly shape the active weight set, making the inference working set larger, more diverse, and harder to manage efficiently.

%
% v1: Large-scale LLM serving is increasingly shaped by the convergence of two trends that are each effective in isolation but jointly challenging in deployment: sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) base models~\cite{todo:moe-llm} and LoRA-based multi-tenant adaptation~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. In production settings, these trends naturally meet in \emph{multi-LoRA MoE serving}. While LoRA is widely used as a lightweight mechanism for tenant-specific customization, existing multi-LoRA serving systems have largely been designed for dense-model adaptation rather than expert-layer adaptation in sparse MoE models~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. Extending LoRA to MoE expert layers is both natural and practically important, because expert FFN blocks account for a large fraction of model capacity and provide a high-leverage target for task- or tenant-specific specialization~\cite{todo:moe-knowledge-capacity, schulman2025lora}. This combination is appealing from a deployment perspective: MoE reduces base-model compute, while LoRA enables efficient per-tenant customization without replicating the full model. However, it also creates a distinct serving regime in which dynamic sparse routing~\cite{todo:moe-routing-dynamics} and long-tailed multi-tenant adaptation~\cite{todo:slora} jointly determine which expert- and adapter-side weights are needed for each request, increasing access diversity and complicating locality management during inference.

This enlarged and more diverse working set becomes especially problematic during \emph{decode} in prefill--decode deployments~\cite{todo:pd-serving}. Unlike prefill, which can often amortize weight-loading costs across many prompt tokens, decode operates under tight inter-token latency SLOs: generation is highly memory-bandwidth bound, and any weight miss on the critical path directly translates to pipeline stalls and ITL degradation. Consequently, the granularity of weight management becomes critical: in pure MoE serving, the natural unit is the expert; in conventional multi-LoRA serving, it is the adapter, and prior systems such as S-LoRA~\cite{todo:slora} and VaLoRA~\cite{mi2025empower} therefore adopt adapter-centric designs that assume dense adapter loading. In multi-LoRA MoE decode, however, a request only needs the LoRA residuals for the \emph{selected} experts, so the effective unit of access and reuse is neither an expert alone nor an adapter alone, but a joint expert--LoRA object. These objects are substantially larger than the attention-side LoRA units emphasized in prior systems, because expert-layer LoRA scales with the FFN intermediate dimension (typically 4$\times$--8$\times$ the model width), whereas attention-side LoRA targets the narrower head projections~\cite{todo:moe-ffn-architecture}. At the same time, the base MoE model typically already occupies most device memory, leaving only limited residual VRAM for caching such objects~\cite{todo:large-moe-models}. This breaks the locality assumptions of prior caches: the enlarged and fragmented working set prevents concentration of hot expert--lora pairs, leading to cache thrashing and unpredictable decode latency.
% v2: This enlarged and more diverse working set becomes especially problematic during \emph{decode} in prefill--decode deployments~\cite{todo:pd-serving}. Unlike prefill, which can often amortize weight-loading costs across many prompt tokens, decode operates one token at a time: effective batch sizes are small, and a single miss on the per-token critical path is directly exposed as token latency. This makes the unit of weight management especially important. In pure MoE serving, that unit is naturally the expert; in conventional multi-LoRA serving, it is the adapter, and prior systems such as S-LoRA~\cite{todo:slora} and VaLoRA~\cite{mi2025empower} therefore use adapter-centric designs. In multi-LoRA MoE decode, however, a request only needs the LoRA residuals for the \emph{selected} experts, so the effective unit of access and reuse is neither an expert alone nor an adapter alone, but a joint expert--LoRA object. These objects are substantially larger than the attention-side LoRA units emphasized in prior multi-LoRA systems, because LoRA attached to MoE expert FFN blocks scales with the wide feed-forward dimensions rather than the narrower attention projections~\cite{todo:moe-ffn-architecture}. At the same time, the base MoE model typically already occupies most device memory, leaving only limited residual VRAM for caching such objects~\cite{todo:large-moe-models}. The result is a different locality regime for decode: the effective working set is both enlarged and fragmented, weakening the concentrated hot set that conventional sparse-serving caches depend on.
%
% v1: This expanded and more diverse working set is especially problematic during \emph{decode} in prefill--decode deployments~\cite{todo:pd-serving}. Prefill can often amortize weight-loading costs across many prompt tokens, but decode exposes them directly: generation proceeds one token at a time, effective batch sizes are small, and any miss on the per-token execution path is immediately reflected in token latency. In pure MoE serving, the natural unit of management is the expert, while in conventional multi-LoRA serving it is the adapter; accordingly, prior systems such as S-LoRA~\cite{todo:slora} and VaLoRA~\cite{mi2025empower} adopt adapter-centric designs. In multi-LoRA MoE decode, however, a request only needs the LoRA residuals associated with the \emph{selected} experts. The effective unit of access and reuse is therefore neither an expert alone nor an adapter alone, but a joint expert--LoRA object. This shift is important because expert-layer LoRA is materially larger than the attention-layer LoRA targeted by most prior multi-LoRA systems. In transformer MoE models, LoRA attached to expert FFN blocks scales with the wide feed-forward dimensions rather than the narrower attention projections~\cite{todo:moe-ffn-architecture}. As a result, each expert--LoRA object occupies substantially more memory, while only limited residual GPU memory remains available for caching because the base MoE model itself is typically kept resident on device~\cite{todo:large-moe-models}. Multi-LoRA MoE decode therefore shifts the cache locality regime: the effective working set becomes both larger and more fragmented, weakening the concentrated hot set on which conventional sparse-serving caches rely.

To quantify the locality regime introduced by multi-LoRA MoE decode, we conduct a trace-driven study using Alibaba LoRA serving traces augmented with realistic MoE expert routing patterns~\cite{lin2025understanding}. The study shows that once access is modeled at the granularity of joint expert--LoRA objects, the hot set becomes markedly less concentrated. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}(a), the top-1K objects account for 89.1\% of accesses under expert-only granularity, but only 41.4\% and 33.1\% under joint-granularity modeling with independent (C1) and correlated (C2) adapter-expert assignment, respectively. This reduced concentration makes cache scaling far less effective: in Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}(b), an expert-only oracle reaches near-ideal P99 TPOT with a cache budget of just 2K objects, whereas realistic joint-object workloads require up to 16$\times$ more cache slots to reach the same target. Under a cache budget sufficient for expert-only modeling to reach diminishing returns, the penalty shifts to the extreme tail: median TPOT remains near 1.2\,ms, while P99 TPOT rises to 7.06\,ms, a roughly 6$\times$ slowdown (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}(c)). Together, these results show that in multi-LoRA MoE decode, capacity misses are not transient anomalies that can be eliminated by modest cache growth; they are persistent tail events on the decode critical path.

The results show that multi-LoRA MoE decode substantially weakens the access concentration that conventional sparse-serving caches depend on. These results indicate that in this regime, cold misses are not rare anomalies that can be eliminated by modest cache growth; they are persistent tail events on the decode critical path.

Once GPU capacity misses become unavoidable, the central problem shifts from \emph{how to avoid misses} to \emph{how to serve them on the decode critical path}. Existing GPU-centric systems typically handle a miss with a load-then-run policy: the required weights are first promoted from host memory to GPU memory, and execution resumes only after that promotion completes~\cite{todo:gpu-offload}. This approach is effective when misses are infrequent and future reuse is sufficient to amortize migration cost. In multi-LoRA MoE decode, however, a capacity miss often incurs PCIe transfer latency that dwarfs the lightweight LoRA kernel executing for a single token, leaving minimal compute work to amortize transfer latency or guarantee near-term reuse. In this regime, promotion-first recovery fails not merely due to PCIe bandwidth limits, but because weight transfer becomes a \emph{blocking synchronization point} that directly stalls the token generation pipeline. The resulting systems question is therefore: when a joint expert--LoRA object is GPU-cold, should the current token stall for synchronous promotion, or should the miss take a differetnt execution path?
% v2: Once GPU-cold misses become unavoidable, the central problem is no longer only how to avoid misses, but how to serve them on the decode critical path. Existing GPU-centric systems typically handle a miss with a load-then-run policy: the required weights are first promoted from host memory to GPU memory, and execution resumes only after that promotion completes~\cite{todo:gpu-offload}. This approach is effective when misses are infrequent and future reuse is sufficient to amortize migration cost. In multi-LoRA MoE decode, however, a GPU-cold miss may be triggered by only a small amount of LoRA-side computation for a single token, under small effective batch sizes and uncertain immediate reuse. Under these conditions, the main problem with promotion-first recovery is not just transfer bandwidth. It is that weight promotion is exposed directly as a \emph{blocking synchronization point} in token generation. The resulting systems question is therefore: when a joint expert--LoRA object is GPU-cold, should the current token stall for synchronous promotion, or should the miss take a different execution path?
%
% v1: Once GPU-cold misses become unavoidable, the core problem is no longer only \emph{how to avoid misses}, but \emph{how to serve them efficiently when they occur}. Existing GPU-centric systems typically recover from a miss using a load-then-run policy, that is, a blocking weight-promotion path in which the required weights are first migrated from host memory to GPU memory and execution resumes only after promotion completes~\cite{todo:gpu-offload}. This strategy works well when misses are infrequent and the cost of promotion can be amortized by subsequent reuse. In multi-LoRA MoE decode, however, a GPU-cold miss often corresponds to a relatively small amount of LoRA-side computation on the critical path of a single token, with limited batch-level amortization and uncertain near-term reuse. In this regime, the problem with promotion-first recovery is not simply PCIe bandwidth consumption; it is that the miss becomes a \emph{blocking synchronization point} for the current token. The key systems question therefore becomes: when a joint expert--LoRA object is not resident on the GPU, should the current token synchronously wait for promotion, or should the miss be served through a different execution path?

We address this problem with CoLoRA, a decode-time runtime for multi-LoRA MoE serving that replaces blocking promotion-first recovery with execution-first heterogeneous miss handling. CoLoRA uses a residency-aware hot/cold dual-path design for expert--LoRA computation during decode. Cache-resident adapters remain on the GPU hot path, while GPU-cold adapters are handled through a separate cold path rather than triggering immediate synchronous promotion. Crucially, CoLoRA does not offload the full expert computation to the CPU, nor does it assume host execution is generally faster than GPU execution. Instead, it exploits a decode-time data-movement asymmetry: computing a cold LoRA residual on the CPU exchanges only per-token activation vectors, whereas promotion-first recovery must first transfer the full expert--LoRA weight object to the GPU. The base MoE expert computation therefore remains on the GPU, while the corresponding cold LoRA residual is computed on the CPU from host-resident weights and merged back for the current token. By detaching only the cold LoRA contribution from blocking promotion, CoLoRA treats GPU-cold misses as bounded heterogeneous execution events rather than unconditional migration barriers on the decode critical path.

% v1: We address this problem with \textbf{CoLoRA}, a decode-time serving runtime for multi-LoRA MoE models that replaces blocking promotion-first recovery with execution-first heterogeneous miss handling. CoLoRA adopts a hot/cold dual-path design for expert--LoRA computation during decode. When the required expert--LoRA object is resident in GPU memory, it is served on the GPU hot path. When it is GPU-cold, CoLoRA does not migrate the entire object to the GPU before resuming execution. Nor does it move the full expert computation to the CPU or assume that host execution is generally faster than device execution. Instead, CoLoRA exploits a decode-time asymmetry in data movement: serving a cold LoRA residual on the CPU requires exchanging only per-token activation/state vectors, whereas promotion-first recovery must first transfer the entire expert--LoRA weight object to the GPU. Accordingly, the base MoE expert computation remains on the GPU, while the corresponding cold LoRA residual is computed on the CPU from host-resident weights and merged back for the current token. In this way, CoLoRA detaches only the cold LoRA contribution from blocking promotion, turning GPU-cold misses from unconditional migration barriers into bounded heterogeneous execution events on the decode critical path.

CoLoRA is built on three key ideas. (1) Execution-first residency-aware hot/cold dual-path serving: GPU-resident expert--LoRA objects remain on the hot path, while GPU-cold objects are handled through a separate miss path instead of triggering immediate blocking promotion. (2) Decoupled miss recovery through a CPU cold path: when an object is GPU-cold, CoLoRA computes only the corresponding LoRA residual via a latency-bounded CPU-side fallback,  keeping the GPU as the primary engine for hot objects and base-model expert computation. (3) Locality-driven background optimization: deferred promotion and selective temporal predispatch improve reuse under fragmented access patterns and overlap cold-path data movement with subsequent hot-path decode steps, ensuring demand execution remains decoupled from prediction accuracy or synchronous migration.

(3) Locality-driven background optimization: deferred promotion and selective temporal predispatch improve future reuse under fragmented locality and partially overlap cold-path latency, without making demand execution rely on perfect prediction or synchronous migration.

Our contributions are threefold:
\begin{itemize}

  \item We identify and characterize a new decode-time GPU-cold-miss regime in multi-LoRA MoE serving. Using trace-driven analysis, we show that when joint expert--LoRA objects become the effective unit of access, locality deteriorates structurally: hot-set concentration weakens, cache capacity scaling yields diminishing returns, and the remaining performance loss shifts into the latency tail.

% v2: \item We identify and characterize a new decode-time GPU-cold-miss regime in multi-LoRA MoE serving. Using trace-driven analysis, we show that when joint expert--LoRA objects become the effective unit of access, locality deteriorates structurally: hot-set concentration weakens, cache scaling becomes markedly less effective, and the remaining performance loss shifts into the latency tail.


 \item We design CoLoRA, a decode-time serving runtime that replaces blocking promotion with execution-first heterogeneous miss handling. CoLoRA integrates a residency-aware hot/cold dual-path scheduler, bounded CPU-side LoRA residual computation, and locality-driven background policies that prefetch and stage objects without stalling demand execution.

  \item We implement CoLoRA in a multi-LoRA MoE serving prototype that supports execution-first cold-miss recovery under realistic cache pressure.......

\end{itemize}

Across trace-driven and end-to-end evaluations, CoLoRA shows that execution-first cold-miss handling improves the robustness of multi-LoRA MoE decode serving under realistic cache pressure. By removing blocking promotion from the critical path of GPU-cold misses, CoLoRA reduces tail-latency inflation while preserving efficient GPU execution for hot objects and base-model computation.

\section{Background, Motivation, and Challenges}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{Background: Expert--LoRA Computation in Multi-LoRA MoE Decode}
\label{subsec:background}

In decode-time serving of large language models, combining a shared sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) base model with multiple LoRA specializations introduces a complex, fine-grained parameter access pattern. During decode, each generated token triggers dynamic routing within the base model, while concurrent requests invoke different, task-specific LoRA adapters. Consequently, the serving system must repeatedly resolve both the activated experts and the adapter-specific LoRA states on the latency-critical decode path.

This interaction changes the natural unit at which the system should reason about locality and misses. In dense multi-LoRA serving, accesses often concentrate on a single adapter's weights, making adapter-level reasoning sufficient in many cases. In MoE decode, however, each token activates only a small routed subset of experts, and LoRA computation is needed only for the routed experts of the current request. The relevant access unit is therefore not an expert or an adapter in isolation, but their joint occurrence in the decode path, which we refer to as an \emph{expert--LoRA joint object}.

This distinction matters particularly in decode. Decode operates at small effective batch sizes, repeats routing and parameter-access decisions once per token, and exposes miss-handling overheads directly on the latency-critical path. Consequently, when expert--LoRA joint objects do not fit cleanly within practical GPU cache budgets, the key systems question is not only how to manage residency, but also how to recover cold misses without inflating per-token latency.


\subsection{Motivation: Joint-Object Modeling Fragments Decode Locality}
\label{subsec:motivation}

\subsubsection{Expert--LoRA Joint Objects as the Relevant Access Unit}
\label{subsec:joint-object}

A central question is what abstraction the system should use to reason about locality, residency, and misses.

In sparse MoE decode, each token activates only a small subset of routed experts. Once multiple LoRA adapters coexist, accesses no longer concentrate on entire adapters or on experts alone, but on LoRA states attached to specific routed experts. This makes expert--LoRA joint objects the relevant access unit for decode-time serving.

Reasoning at coarser granularity obscures the true access pattern. Adapter-level management is too coarse because it retains many expert slices together with the few that are actually needed for the current token. Expert-level management is incomplete in multi-tenant serving because it ignores adapter identity: while the expert set is fixed, LoRA adapters vary across requests, so collapsing accesses by expert alone systematically overestimates reuse across tenants. To understand the consequences of this change in access granularity, we next compare decode locality and system behavior under expert-only and expert--LoRA joint-object conditions.


\subsubsection{Joint Objects Fragment Decode Locality}
\label{subsec:case-study}

To examine whether this finer-grained access view matters in practice, we conduct a trace-driven case study under three workload conditions.
\texttt{C0} uses expert-only keys.
\texttt{C1} uses expert--LoRA joint keys under independent assignment, where adapter identity is sampled independently of expert routing.
\texttt{C2} uses the same expert--LoRA joint keys under correlated assignment, where certain adapters are more likely to co-occur with specific experts.
This setup separates the effect of finer-grained keying itself from the extent to which structured adapter--expert affinity can partially preserve locality.
We use Alibaba trace~\cite{lin2025understanding} to model LoRA serving request arrivals and LoRA invocations, and replay the resulting decode access streams under these conditions.

As illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}, modeling accesses as joint objects triggers a cascade of system-level degradations, demonstrating that traditional caching strategies are insufficient for this workload.

\paragraph{Locality breaks under joint objects.}
Moving from coarse-grained to joint-object modeling severely fragments decode locality. Figure \ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}(a) shows that the access distribution flattens substantially when expert routing and adapter identity are modeled jointly. Because the access frequency is distributed across a combinatorial space of expert--lora pairs, the "hot set" shrinks in dominance. Consequently, a bounded GPU cache captures a significantly smaller fraction of total accesses, leading to longer reuse distances and frequent cold starts.

\paragraph{Cache scaling loses effectiveness.}
Because locality is fundamentally fragmented, simply increasing GPU cache capacity fails to resolve the issue. Figure \ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}(b) demonstrates the diminishing returns of capacity scaling. Under joint-object access patterns, the system requires up to 16x more cached objects to match the P99 latency of an expert-only oracle. Over-provisioning high-bandwidth memory to this degree is economically and architecturally infeasible, meaning systems must operate under constrained budgets where cache misses are inevitable.

\paragraph{Tail latency explodes under misses.}
The most severe consequence of this locality fragmentation manifests in request latency. Figure \ref{fig:motivation-breakdown}(c) evaluates Time Per Output Token (TPOT) under a practical GPU cache budget. While the median TPOT remains near-optimal at approximately 1.2 ms, the degradation is heavily concentrated in the tail. P99.9 latency increases by roughly 6x. Because decode operations repeat routing and parameter-access decisions token by token, cold misses stall the synchronous execution path, disproportionately penalizing tail requests that happen to traverse un-cached expert–adapter intersections.

Taken together, these results show that the key problem in multi-LoRA MoE decode is no longer only cache efficiency in the traditional sense. Once expert--LoRA joint objects become the effective unit of access, the remaining performance loss is increasingly determined by how unavoidable cold misses are handled on the decode critical path.

\subsection{Challenges}
\label{subsec:challenges}

The empirical results above reveal a fundamental shift in the role of caching for multi-LoRA MoE decode serving. Once expert--LoRA joint objects become the effective unit of access, locality degradation makes cold misses difficult to eliminate within practical GPU cache capacity alone. Cold misses are therefore no longer rare anomalies that can be absorbed by a sufficiently large hot set. Instead, they become persistent events on the latency-critical decode path, and the dominant systems question shifts from how to avoid every miss to how to recover unavoidable misses without inflating per-token latency.

Realizing this shift in a practical serving runtime requires addressing three challenges.

\paragraph{Challenge 1: Reasoning at expert--LoRA granularity under expanded and fragmented working sets.}
\label{subsec:challenge-residency}

Under joint-object modeling, the effective key space expands substantially, while reuse becomes weaker and more fragmented across requests. This makes coarse-grained management ineffective: adapter-level residency retains many expert slices that are never touched, whereas expert-only reasoning overestimates reuse by ignoring adapter diversity. At the same time, naive fine-grained residency increases fragmentation pressure on the effective hot set and makes limited GPU capacity more vulnerable to transient cold objects.

The system must therefore reason at expert--LoRA granularity, which matches actual computation, without assuming that caching alone can absorb the resulting working-set expansion.

\paragraph{Challenge 2: Recovering cold misses without forcing promotion-first stalls on decode.}
\label{subsec:challenge-miss}

In this regime, many misses correspond to cold objects whose near-term reuse is too limited to amortize immediate promotion. If the system continues to apply a conventional load-then-run policy, each such miss becomes a blocking recovery event: the current token must wait for weight migration before expert--LoRA computation can proceed. Under decode-time latency sensitivity, this directly amplifies tail latency.

The system therefore needs a different default recovery strategy for cold misses. Instead of forcing all misses through immediate GPU promotion, it must provide a way to complete the current expert--LoRA computation without making promotion the only recovery path, while still preserving the option to promote objects later when future reuse justifies it.

\paragraph{Challenge 3: Making cold-path recovery practical under decode constraints.}
\label{subsec:challenge-overlap}

Changing the miss-recovery abstraction is not sufficient by itself. If cold-path execution is too slow, the system merely replaces GPU promotion stall with CPU-side stall. If it is poorly integrated with the decode pipeline, heterogeneous execution introduces a new source of queueing and tail behavior rather than alleviating the original one.

The system must therefore make cold-path recovery efficient enough to operate at small, irregular decode batch sizes, and organize execution to preserve opportunities for overlap between cold-miss handling and GPU hot-path or base-model computation whenever dependencies allow. The challenge is not only to provide an alternative recovery path, but to ensure that this path reduces exposed miss latency instead of becoming a new bottleneck.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/architecture.pdf}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Hot/Cold Execution-First Architecture}
\label{subsec:dual-path-handling}

CoLoRA is motivated by a simple observation: under multi-tenant expert--LoRA serving, cold misses cannot be treated as rare exceptions. Once the unit of management becomes the expert--LoRA joint object, the effective working set expands and fragments, and misses remain common under realistic GPU memory budgets. In decode, where execution proceeds token by token and batching opportunities are limited, each such miss can directly surface as a stall on the current token's critical path.

The design objective is therefore not to eliminate every miss, but to prevent a cold miss from becoming a global synchronization event. CoLoRA does so by changing the default recovery action. Instead of synchronously restoring missing weights to the GPU and only then resuming execution, it adopts an execution-first policy: the system prioritizes completing the missing expert--LoRA computation using immediately available resources, while treating weight promotion as a separate optimization for future reuse.

More broadly, CoLoRA is built around a uniform design philosophy: the mechanism that guarantees progress for the current token should be separated from the mechanisms that improve locality for future tokens. This separation allows miss handling to remain latency-oriented and correctness-critical, while promotion and prefetching remain opportunistic optimizations rather than mandatory recovery steps.

This leads to a hot/cold dual-path design for expert--LoRA computation in decode. When the required expert--LoRA object is resident, execution proceeds on the GPU hot path with no change to the normal fast path. When the object is absent, the request is diverted to a CPU cold path that completes the current LoRA computation using host-resident parameters. The key point is that the miss no longer forces the entire execution group to wait for immediate promotion.

The runtime realizes this behavior through a skip-and-reinsert discipline. If request $i$ encounters a miss at layer $L$, it is temporarily removed from the current GPU execution group, and its activation state is staged for host-side execution. The GPU then continues processing other ready requests at the same layer without waiting. Once the CPU cold path finishes the missing expert--LoRA computation, the result is returned to the device and request $i$ resumes from the next execution point. In effect, a cold miss delays only the affected request, rather than serializing all requests that happened to be grouped with it.

This design preserves three invariants that are central to correctness. First, each request still advances strictly in layer order. Second, different requests are allowed to be temporarily out of phase, which creates room for overlap rather than forcing lockstep execution. Third, a miss in one request does not block the progress of other ready requests. Together, these invariants allow CoLoRA to convert unavoidable misses from global stalls into localized delay.

The design is particularly well matched to decode-time serving, where per-adapter batch sizes are small, routing decisions are heterogeneous across requests, and misses are not perfectly synchronized. In this regime, even modest overlap between hot-path GPU execution and cold-path CPU execution can substantially reduce the visible impact of cold misses. The next subsection therefore examines the cost structure of this execution-first recovery path and clarifies why its critical-path placement is more favorable than promotion-first recovery.

\subsection{Cost Structure of Cold-Path Execution}
\label{subsec:analytical-formulation}

Execution-first miss handling replaces synchronous weight promotion with a sequence that moves activations to the host, computes the missing LoRA contribution there, and returns the result to the device. The latency of a cold-path invocation can be decomposed as
\begin{equation}
T_{\text{cold}} = T_{\text{pack}} + T_{\text{D2H}} + T_{\text{cpu}} + T_{\text{H2D}} + T_{\text{merge}},
\end{equation}
where $T_{\text{pack}}$ denotes activation packing and layout preparation, $T_{\text{D2H}}$ and $T_{\text{H2D}}$ are device-to-host and host-to-device transfers, $T_{\text{cpu}}$ is host-side computation, and $T_{\text{merge}}$ is the cost of reintegrating the result into the device-side execution stream.

This decomposition matters because, in decode, the transferred activation payload is typically much smaller than the missing expert--LoRA weights themselves. As a result, execution-first avoids placing full weight movement on the current token's critical path. The dominant concern is therefore not whether the CPU path is universally faster in absolute time, but whether enough of its latency can be overlapped with ongoing GPU work on other requests.

For comparison, a promotion-first recovery path incurs
\begin{equation}
T_{\text{promote}} = T_{\text{admit}} + T_{\text{H2D-weights}} + T_{\text{gpu}},
\end{equation}
where $T_{\text{admit}}$ captures admission and scheduling overheads for the restored object, $T_{\text{H2D-weights}}$ is the host-to-device transfer of weights, and $T_{\text{gpu}}$ is the subsequent GPU execution. In expert--LoRA serving, the transfer and preparation of weights are often the dominant terms. More importantly, promotion-first keeps those costs on the synchronous recovery path of the current token.

The central distinction, then, is not merely one of total latency but of critical-path placement. Promotion-first makes recovery latency visible immediately because execution must wait for residency restoration. Execution-first instead turns recovery into a parallel side path whose visible cost is reduced whenever the hot path still has useful work to perform. This observation directly informs the runtime design: CoLoRA must minimize fixed per-miss overheads, keep cold-path execution bounded and predictable, and preserve overlap whenever ready GPU work remains. We next describe the scheduler that realizes this decoupling in the runtime.

\subsection{Decoupled Miss-Recovery Scheduler}
\label{subsec:scheduler}

The execution-first design depends on a runtime scheduler that explicitly decouples cold-miss handling from the main GPU execution stream. Conceptually, each request alternates among three states: it is either ready to execute on the GPU hot path, being processed on the CPU cold path after a miss, or waiting to be reinserted once a cold-path result has returned. The scheduler maintains corresponding queues for GPU-ready work, CPU cold-path jobs, and completed results awaiting reintegration.

When a miss occurs at layer $L$, the scheduler removes the affected request from the GPU-ready set, materializes its activations into a staging buffer, and submits a cold-path job to the CPU side. Crucially, the GPU does not wait for this job to complete. It immediately continues issuing kernels for the remaining ready requests. When the cold-path job finishes, the result is transferred back to device memory and the request is reintroduced into GPU execution at the appropriate continuation point.

This organization gives the system \emph{decoupled miss recovery}: GPU progress is no longer tied to immediate weight promotion for every cold object. More precisely, the request that incurs the miss still waits for its own cold-path result before it can advance, but other ready requests do not need to synchronize on that recovery. CoLoRA therefore does not eliminate cold-miss latency; instead, it isolates that latency to the faulting request and prevents a single miss from turning into a group-wide stall.

To keep the cold path from turning into an uncontrolled source of backlog, CoLoRA uses an explicit bound on cold-path concurrency. Only a limited number of cold jobs may be in flight at once, and excess misses are queued rather than launched immediately. This keeps host-side resource usage predictable and avoids replacing one form of global instability with another. Within this bounded regime, the scheduler preserves per-request layer ordering, allows cross-request phase decoupling, and maintains forward progress on the GPU whenever ready work exists.

This scheduler is the runtime embodiment of CoLoRA's core philosophy: demand execution is serviced immediately through the hot path or the cold path, while all other optimizations remain secondary to forward progress. Realizing that philosophy in practice, however, requires a cold path whose overheads are low and predictable enough to overlap with useful GPU work.

\subsection{CPU Cold Path Realization}
\label{subsec:cpu-cold-path}

The CPU cold path is designed not as a throughput replacement for the GPU, but as a predictable execution engine for unavoidable misses. Its job is to make execution-first recovery viable in decode by keeping miss handling bounded, overlap-friendly, and implementation-efficient.

The first step is activation packing. Before a cold-path transfer is issued, the relevant activations are reorganized on the GPU into contiguous staging buffers. This activation coalescing reduces fragmentation in DMA traffic and amortizes transfer overheads when multiple cold-path requests can be handled together. Because decode activations are relatively small, careful packing matters not only for bandwidth efficiency, but also for reducing fixed per-miss overheads.

Transfers between device and host use pinned memory and are issued asynchronously on separate CUDA streams. This allows device-to-host activation movement and host-to-device result return to overlap opportunistically with foreground GPU work, subject to available copy-engine capacity and scheduler state. The goal is not to assume perfect overlap, but to preserve it whenever the hardware and workload permit.

On the host side, missing expert--LoRA computations are executed by vectorized CPU kernels. CoLoRA uses AVX-optimized implementations for the dense linear operations involved in LoRA execution, binds worker threads to dedicated cores to reduce scheduling jitter, and NUMA-aligns those workers with the GPU's PCIe root complex when applicable. These choices are intended to keep $T_{\text{cpu}}$ stable and predictable under repeated decode-time invocations. The system does not rely on the claim that CPU execution is generally faster than GPU execution. Instead, it relies on the more realistic and more important claim that the cold path can be made sufficiently efficient and sufficiently stable to overlap with useful GPU work in mixed hit/miss batches.

Once the host computation completes, the result is copied back and merged into the device-side execution state. This reintegration step is deliberately lightweight and avoids introducing a global barrier. In combination, activation coalescing, asynchronous staging, and vectorized host execution turn the CPU into a practical cold-path engine rather than a fallback of last resort.

With this execution substrate in place, CoLoRA can cleanly separate the mechanism that serves a miss now from the mechanisms that improve how likely similar accesses are to be served more efficiently later. We therefore turn to the locality-driven optimizations layered on top of the execution-first core.

\subsection{Locality-Driven Background Optimizations}
\label{subsec:locality-background}

Beyond execution-first miss recovery, CoLoRA incorporates two locality-driven background optimizations that improve future access efficiency without reintroducing promotion-first behavior on the current token's critical path.

The first is deferred promotion. While CoLoRA removes blocking promotion from the foreground miss-recovery path, promotion remains important for improving future GPU residency. The key design change is therefore not to eliminate promotion, but to redefine its role. In CoLoRA, promotion no longer serves as the default recovery mechanism for the current miss. Instead, it is treated as a background optimization whose purpose is to increase the likelihood that subsequent accesses are served on the GPU hot path.

When a cold-path execution is triggered, CoLoRA may asynchronously enqueue the corresponding expert--LoRA object for promotion into GPU memory. This promotion is issued off the critical path and does not delay completion of the current token. In effect, cold-path execution handles the present access, while deferred promotion improves cache residency for future accesses if the object is likely to be reused.

To prevent promotion from degenerating into indiscriminate background traffic, CoLoRA employs a reuse-distance-aware admission policy. Let $\delta$ denote a reuse threshold. An object is admitted for asynchronous promotion only when it is expected to be reused within the next $\delta$ decode steps. Objects whose predicted reuse distance exceeds $\delta$ remain host-resident and continue to be served on demand through the cold path. This policy avoids wasting PCIe bandwidth and GPU cache capacity on weakly reusable objects, and preserves the benefit of removing blocking promotion from the foreground execution path.

In the current design, $\delta$ is implemented as a static hyperparameter. A more adaptive policy that tunes $\delta$ online based on runtime signals, such as observed reuse behavior, PCIe queue depth, or device-memory pressure, is left to future work. Importantly, admission errors affect only future cache efficiency: they do not delay the current request and do not alter CoLoRA's execution-first miss-handling semantics.

The second optimization exploits short-horizon temporal locality in decode to reduce effective cold-path service time. Our router traces show that consecutive decode tokens exhibit strong but layer-dependent routing continuity: the mean expert-set hit rate is 72.2\% overall, with early layers exceeding 95\%, middle layers dipping to 56.8\%, and late layers recovering to 87\% (Appendix~\ref{app:temporal-locality}, Figure~\ref{fig:temporal_locality_hit_rate}). Although long-horizon reuse of expert--LoRA objects can be weak under multi-tenant serving, this U-shaped per-layer profile still indicates that near-future accesses are substantially more predictable than global cache behavior might suggest.

CoLoRA leverages this regularity using a lightweight temporal predictor that identifies expert candidates likely to be accessed in the next few decode steps and opportunistically prefetches the corresponding host-resident weights. The layer dependence of the trace signal suggests that this predictor should be viewed as an opportunistic background policy rather than an always-on dependency for forward progress. Importantly, prefetching does not participate in demand execution: a request never waits for a prefetched object, and cold-path execution remains the default fallback when the required object is not yet available. The purpose of this mechanism is therefore not to guarantee stable residency in any particular CPU cache level, nor to assume that large expert weights remain fully resident in LLC. Rather, it improves effective access locality and reduces the service time of subsequent cold-path invocations when the prediction is correct.
% TODO: 是否需要说明 prefetch 的对象很小 ~几百KB level，所以足以放在 LLC 上而不影响别的计算？

Because temporal prefetching is auxiliary to the main execution-first design, incorrect predictions consume only bounded background bandwidth and do not affect correctness or foreground progress. Taken together, deferred promotion and temporal prefetching preserve CoLoRA's uniform design philosophy: misses are served immediately through execution-first recovery, while locality-driven background mechanisms optimize how similar accesses are handled later.

\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:evaluation}

% Suggested artifact order:
% Table 1: Experimental setup and default parameters.
% Figure 1: Synthetic locality breakdown and cache scaling.
% Figure 2: Synthetic latency percentiles under controlled miss pressure.

This section evaluates CoLoRA from two complementary angles. 
We first use synthetic workloads to isolate the decode-time cold-miss regime introduced by expert--LoRA joint objects and to stress the system under controlled cache budgets, popularity skew, and request rates. We then move to a live-server evaluation driven by Alibaba traces and ShareGPT v3 prompts to validate end-to-end behavior under realistic multi-tenant serving conditions. Unless otherwise noted, we focus on decode-time behavior because CoLoRA targets cold-miss recovery on the token-generation critical path.

\subsection{Evaluation Questions}
\label{sec:eval_questions}

We answer the following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Q1: Locality regime.}
    Does modeling accesses at expert--LoRA joint-object granularity materially weaken hot-set concentration and reduce the effectiveness of cache scaling?

    \item \textbf{Q2: Miss-handling effectiveness.}
    Under controlled cold-miss pressure, does execution-first recovery reduce tail-latency inflation compared with promotion-first load-then-run recovery?

    \item \textbf{Q3: End-to-end serving gains.}
    Under realistic replay with Alibaba traces and ShareGPT v3 prompts, does CoLoRA improve tail TPOT and SLO attainment while preserving average latency
    and throughput?

    \item \textbf{Q4: Component contributions.}
    How much do the CPU cold path, deferred promotion, and temporal predispatch each contribute to the final gains?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:eval_setup}

\paragraph{Prototype and Hardware.}
We implement CoLoRA in our multi-LoRA MoE serving prototype and evaluate it on
a server equipped with \textit{[CPU model]}, \textit{[GPU model]}, and
\textit{[host memory size]}.  Unless otherwise specified, all results are
measured on a single-node deployment.  We report additional multi-GPU results
only if they are needed to demonstrate scalability beyond the main claim.

\paragraph{Model and Adaptation Setup.}
We evaluate on \textit{[base MoE model name]} with LoRA attached to
\textit{[targeted expert FFN layers / expert projections]}.
We use \textit{[LoRA rank(s)]}, \textit{[number of experts]}, and
\textit{[precision / quantization setting]}.
The effective cache object is an expert--LoRA joint object.
We explicitly report its size so that cache budgets can be interpreted in both
``number of objects'' and ``GPU memory footprint''.

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against the following systems:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Promotion-First}: the same serving stack, but with
    conventional load-then-run recovery, i.e., a cold object is first promoted
    to GPU memory and only then executed.

    \item \textbf{CoLoRA}: the full system with hot/cold dual-path execution,
    bounded CPU cold-path execution, deferred promotion, and temporal
    predispatch.

    \item \textbf{CoLoRA w/o Deferred Promotion}: disables asynchronous
    promotion to isolate the benefit of future-reuse optimization.

    \item \textbf{CoLoRA w/o Temporal Predispatch}: disables short-horizon
    predispatch to isolate the benefit of overlap-oriented background
    optimization.

    \item \textbf{CoLoRA w/o Cold-Path Optimizations}: disables one or more
    implementation optimizations in the CPU cold path (e.g., activation
    coalescing, pinned staging, or AVX kernels) to measure how much engineering
    is required to make execution-first practical.
\end{itemize}

% \begin{itemize}
%     \item \textbf{Expert-Only Oracle}: a synthetic-only reference that ignores
%     adapter identity and serves as a best-case cache-locality upper bound.
% \end{itemize}

\paragraph{Metrics.}
Our primary metric is \textbf{time per output token (TPOT)}, reported at
P50/P95/P99/P99.9.
We also report \textbf{throughput}, \textbf{SLO attainment},
\textbf{end-to-end request latency}, and \textbf{GPU/CPU miss-handling
statistics}, including cold-path invocation rate, promotion traffic, and GPU
residency hit rate.
Because CoLoRA changes execution scheduling rather than model semantics, we
add a small correctness check by comparing outputs or logits against the
promotion-first baseline on a held-out request set.

\paragraph{Workloads.}
We organize the evaluation around two main workload scenarios:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Synthetic:} controlled workloads used to diagnose locality
    fragmentation and stress miss handling.

    \item \textbf{Live server:} realistic replay using Alibaba traces for
    arrivals/tenant activity and ShareGPT v3 for prompt and response behavior.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Scenario I: Synthetic Stress Tests}
\label{sec:eval_synthetic}

This scenario is diagnosis-first.
Its goal is not realism by itself, but to expose \emph{why} cold misses become
unavoidable and \emph{when} execution-first recovery helps most.

\subsubsection{Synthetic Workload Generator}
\label{sec:eval_synth_gen}

We generate synthetic decode workloads with controllable parameters:
request rate $\lambda$, active-tenant count $N$, adapter popularity skew
$\alpha$, GPU cache budget $B$, and expert-route continuity $\rho$.
To isolate the locality effect of the access unit, we evaluate three access
models:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{C0 (Expert-Only):} accesses are keyed only by the routed
    expert.
    \item \textbf{C1 (Joint-Independent):} accesses are keyed by expert--LoRA
    joint objects, with independent expert and adapter assignment.
    \item \textbf{C2 (Joint-Correlated):} accesses are keyed by expert--LoRA
    joint objects, with structured expert/adapter affinity.
\end{itemize}

For synthetic latency stress tests, we either fix prompt/output lengths or draw
them from narrow distributions so that the observed differences primarily reflect
cache locality and miss-handling behavior rather than unrelated prompt-length
variance.

\subsubsection{Locality Breakdown and Cache Scaling}
\label{sec:eval_synth_locality}

We begin by quantifying how the access distribution changes when the serving
system reasons at expert--LoRA joint-object granularity.
Figure~\ref{fig:synthetic_locality} should contain two panels:
(i) cumulative access fraction versus object rank, and
(ii) P99 TPOT versus cache budget.

% Main message:
% Joint-object modeling flattens the access distribution and makes cache scaling
% much less effective than in expert-only reasoning.

\paragraph{What to show.}
We recommend reporting:
(i) hot-set concentration curves for C0/C1/C2,
(ii) cache budget versus P99 TPOT,
and (iii) the cache-capacity gap needed to recover the same tail target under
expert-only versus joint-object access patterns.

\paragraph{What this subsection should conclude.}
The conclusion should be that the core issue is not merely ``insufficient GPU
capacity,'' but that at expert--LoRA granularity the remaining misses are hard
to eliminate by cache scaling alone.

\subsubsection{Tail Latency Under Controlled Miss Pressure}
\label{sec:eval_synth_tail}

We next evaluate whether CoLoRA reduces tail inflation once cold misses are
present.
Figure~\ref{fig:synthetic_tail} should compare TPOT percentiles under
increasing miss pressure by varying one stress knob at a time:
cache budget, request rate, or active-tenant count.

\paragraph{What to compare.}
The key comparison here is \textbf{Promotion-First} versus \textbf{CoLoRA},
with P50/P95/P99/P99.9 TPOT reported together.
If space allows, also add SLO attainment under a decode-latency target.

\paragraph{What this subsection should conclude.}
The conclusion should be that CoLoRA does not necessarily change the median
dramatically, but it suppresses the \emph{tail amplification} caused by
promotion-first recovery on unavoidable cold misses.

\subsubsection{Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:eval_synth_sensitivity}

To show robustness, we vary the main synthetic knobs one at a time:

\begin{itemize}
    \item GPU cache budget;
    \item request rate;
    \item active-tenant count;
    \item popularity skew;
    \item expert-route continuity;
    \item CPU cold-path worker count / queue depth.
\end{itemize}

This subsection can be short if the curves are monotonic.
Its purpose is to show that CoLoRA's gains persist across a broad miss-pressure
regime rather than only at a single operating point.

\subsection{Scenario II: Live-Server Evaluation with Alibaba Trace + ShareGPT v3}
\label{sec:eval_live}

This scenario is realism-first.
Its goal is to validate that the synthetic conclusions survive in an end-to-end
online serving environment with realistic arrival patterns and prompt behavior.

\subsubsection{Replay Methodology}
\label{sec:eval_live_replay}

We deploy the full system as a live server and replay a multi-tenant workload.
Alibaba traces provide request arrivals and tenant activity patterns, while
ShareGPT v3 provides realistic prompts and response-length behavior.
Each incoming request is assigned a tenant/adaptation identity according to the
trace and is executed end-to-end by the online serving system.

\paragraph{Recommended presentation.}
Be explicit that this is a \emph{server replay}, not an offline simulator.
The value of this section is that it captures queueing, overlap, resource
contention, and scheduler interactions that synthetic experiments intentionally
abstract away.

\subsubsection{End-to-End Latency and Throughput}
\label{sec:eval_live_e2e}

Figure~\ref{fig:live_e2e} should report end-to-end latency and throughput under
increasing offered load.
We suggest one latency figure with P50/P95/P99 TPOT and one throughput/SLO
figure.

\paragraph{What to compare.}
Compare \textbf{Promotion-First}, \textbf{CoLoRA}, and the main ablated variants.
If TTFT is included, keep it secondary; the main claim is decode-tail behavior,
so TPOT should remain the primary axis.

\paragraph{What this subsection should conclude.}
The conclusion should be that CoLoRA preserves the GPU as the fast path for hot
objects while preventing cold misses from turning into severe tail events in the
online system.

\subsubsection{Robustness Under Cache Pressure and Tenant Scale}
\label{sec:eval_live_robustness}

We then vary the practical deployment knobs that determine how often cold misses
occur in production:

\begin{itemize}
    \item GPU cache budget;
    \item number of active tenants / adapters;
    \item offered load;
    \item optional expert fan-out or route diversity if your implementation
    exposes it cleanly.
\end{itemize}

Figure~\ref{fig:live_robustness} should show that CoLoRA degrades more
gracefully than promotion-first recovery as cache pressure increases.

\subsubsection{Operational Breakdown of Miss Recovery}
\label{sec:eval_live_breakdown}

This subsection explains \emph{why} the live-server gains appear.
Figure~\ref{fig:live_breakdown} can include one or more of the following:

\begin{itemize}
    \item a TPOT breakdown into hot-path execution, cold-path execution,
    transfer, and promotion overhead;
    \item a timeline showing overlap among GPU base compute, GPU hot-path LoRA
    compute, and CPU cold-path LoRA compute;
    \item cold-path invocation rate versus promotion traffic;
    \item GPU residency hit rate and promoted-object reuse.
\end{itemize}

This figure is especially important for defending the central claim that the
benefit comes from changing the default miss-recovery action from
promotion-first to execution-first, not merely from adding another cache level.

\subsection{Ablation Studies}
\label{sec:eval_ablation}

After the two main scenarios, we isolate the contribution of each major design
component.

\subsubsection{Execution-First vs.\ Promotion-First}
\label{sec:eval_ablation_execfirst}

This is the core ablation.
Keep the cache budget, workload, and object granularity fixed, and compare only
the miss-recovery policy.
This subsection should make the paper's main takeaway visually obvious.

\subsubsection{CPU Cold-Path Practicality}
\label{sec:eval_ablation_coldpath}

We disable one optimization at a time in the cold path, such as activation
coalescing, pinned staging buffers, or AVX kernels.
The goal is to show that the CPU path is not useful merely because it exists,
but because it is engineered to be predictable and overlap-friendly.

\subsubsection{Deferred Promotion}
\label{sec:eval_ablation_promotion}

We compare full CoLoRA against CoLoRA w/o deferred promotion.
This ablation should answer a narrow question:
does background promotion improve future reuse enough to matter without
reintroducing blocking behavior on the current token's critical path?

\subsubsection{Temporal Predispatch}
\label{sec:eval_ablation_predispatch}

We compare full CoLoRA against CoLoRA w/o temporal predispatch.
Keep this subsection modest in emphasis.
Its purpose is to show that predispatch is a useful auxiliary optimization,
not the main source of the system's benefit.

\subsection{Summary of Findings}
\label{sec:eval_summary}

We summarize the evaluation with three takeaways.
First, once the access unit becomes the expert--LoRA joint object, cache
locality degrades structurally and cold misses remain common under realistic
GPU budgets.
Second, under this regime, promotion-first recovery mainly hurts the latency
tail because the current token must pay for synchronous weight restoration.
Third, CoLoRA's execution-first hot/cold dual-path design reduces that tail
inflation while preserving efficient GPU execution for hot objects and
base-model compute.

\appendix
\section{Per-Layer Temporal Routing Locality}
\label{app:temporal-locality}

Figure~\ref{fig:temporal_locality_hit_rate} reports the per-layer consecutive-token routing locality measured from the Qwen3--VL--MoE router on the ShareGPT--V3 trace. For each request and MoE layer, we compare the routed expert set at decode step $t$ against the previous decode step $t-1$ using the hit-rate metric $|E(L,t) \cap E(L,t-1)| / |E(L,t)|$. The resulting curve is distinctly U-shaped: early layers show very high temporal continuity, middle layers are weaker, and late layers recover. This observation motivates temporal prefetch as a useful but non-uniform optimization across depth.

\begin{figure}[h]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/motivation/temporal_locality_hit_rate.pdf}
  \caption{
  Per-layer consecutive-token routing locality during decode.
  The plotted quantity is the mean expert-set hit rate $|E(L,t) \cap E(L,t-1)| / |E(L,t)|$.
  The curve is U-shaped: early and late layers exhibit stronger temporal continuity, while middle layers are weaker.
  This pattern supports an opportunistic, potentially layer-selective temporal prefetch policy rather than a uniform always-on rule.
  }
  \label{fig:temporal_locality_hit_rate}
\end{figure}
